explain.say: All mammals, from mice to whales, feed their newborns milk made in special glands called mammary glands. That is where the word mammal comes from.

explain.say: When a baby suckles, nerves in the nipple send signals to the mother's brain. The brain releases two hormones: prolactin, which tells the glands to make more milk, and oxytocin, which squeezes the milk out.

explain.say: Milk recipes suit each animal's life. Hooded seal pups nurse for only about four days on milk around 60 percent fat, doubling their weight, while human milk is about 4 percent fat because babies feed often for many months.

faq.a: When a baby suckles, nerve signals reach the mother's brain, which releases the hormone oxytocin. Oxytocin makes tiny muscles around the milk glands squeeze, pushing milk out. This is called the let-down reflex.
Milk is mostly water, with fat for energy, a sugar called lactose, proteins for growth, vitamins and minerals, and antibodies that help protect the baby from infections.
asks: Why is milk good for babies?

faq.q: Why is seal milk so fatty?
faq.a: Seal pups must build a thick layer of blubber fast to survive icy water, and some mothers can nurse for only days. Very fatty milk packs lots of energy into a short time: hooded seal milk is about 60 percent fat.
asks: Which animal has the fattiest milk?
Why do seal pups grow so fast?

faq.a: Yes, every mammal mother makes milk, even the platypus and echidnas, which lay eggs. They have no nipples, so the milk seeps from patches of skin and the young lap it up.
asks: Do whales feed their babies milk?

faq.q: Why is a mother's first milk special?
faq.a: The first milk, called colostrum, is thick and yellowish. It is rich in antibodies and protein, giving the newborn a strong first defence against germs.
asks: Why is the first milk yellow?

facts: Hooded seal pups nurse for only about four days, the shortest nursing period of any mammal.
Platypuses and echidnas lay eggs but still feed their young milk, which seeps from patches of skin.
